description: I’m Vince, a freelance web developer running my own agency with experience building full-stack applications from scratch. I handle everything from frontend integrations and Python backend scripts to managing Linux servers and deploying APIs.
summary:
Imagine living on the Moon and smelling smoke. There’s no door to run out of. Apollo 1 and Mir showed what fire does in a spacecraft, and future Moon and Mars cabins will make it worse: thinner air with 34 % oxygen, and gravity so low that materials burn more easily.

So we asked a simple question: has anyone actually tested that? We mapped all 24 of NASA’s fire experiments. Not one burned a solid material under those conditions.

That’s why we built Black Fox. You pick a cabin, set the air, choose what’s burning, and watch the fire, the smoke and the carbon monoxide spread, in 2D and 3D. A map shows exactly where NASA’s data stops. You can ask our SI anything in plain words, and it backs every answer with the NASA document it came from.

It runs in your browser, with no sign-up. Engineers can check a design before they pay for a physical test, and students can see how fire works off Earth. It doesn’t replace real testing, but it shows which tests matter most.
details:
What it does and how it works

Black Fox is a fire lab for spacecraft and Moon and Mars habitats that runs in your browser. You choose where the cabin is (the ISS, the Gateway, the Moon, Mars or Earth), set the air pressure, oxygen and temperature, and pick what catches fire and where. You also decide how the fans, the alarm and the crew respond. Then you press Start and watch.

Three models run side by side:

  • A cabin model built on NASA-STD-6001 flammability limits, corrected for gravity and airflow. It tells you whether the material will burn, how fast the flame spreads, how much heat it gives off, when the smoke alarm goes off and when carbon monoxide passes NASA’s safety limit.
  • A 2D fire-spread model that follows heat, smoke and oxygen from room to room.
  • A 3D CFD simulation that solves the airflow and the fire in full 3D, right in the browser.

You can also try different extinguishers: CO₂, water mist, potassium aerosol, a clean agent or nitrogen flooding.

Next to the simulator is the research side. We collected all 24 of NASA’s PSI combustion experiments, ranked them for each mission, and drew a “gap map” of where NASA has actually burned materials compared with the air future habitats will use. That map showed us something important: no PSI experiment has burned a solid material in the planned Moon and Mars habitat air (30–34 % oxygen at 56.5–70.3 kPa).

Our SI assistant ties it all together. You can ask it questions in plain words, and it answers using NASA documents, with the source for every claim. It can change the simulation for you (“try it on Mars with less ventilation”), and when you ask where something is, it scrolls the page there and highlights it.

Benefits

Physical fire tests need drop towers or spaceflight, so few teams can run them. Black Fox lets an engineer screen a design in minutes, before paying for a test, and shows which tests matter most. Every number links back to its NASA source, which is what a safety review needs. There’s no sign-up and nothing to install, and it adapts to the device, so it works on an old phone as well as a laptop.

Intended impact

Artemis-era habitats will use thinner air with more oxygen to make spacewalk preparation easier, and that makes fires more dangerous. Most material testing still happens in Earth gravity. We want engineers, researchers, professors and students to see clearly what NASA has tested and what it hasn’t, so the right tests are done before people live there. Long term, the same approach works for sealed spaces on Earth, like aircraft, submarines and mines.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: Python for the backend and physics (FastAPI, Uvicorn); plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the frontend, with no build step; Three.js and WebGL for 3D; Web Workers so the CFD solver doesn’t freeze the page.
  • 3D assets: the habitat module, terrains and lunar globe are generated and baked in Blender from code.
  • Data: NASA Technical Reports Server documents, NASA-STD-6001 limits for 18 materials, the 24 PSI investigations with 1,755 cleaned test rows, and NASA’s carbon monoxide limits (SMAC).
  • SI: open-weight language models (gpt-oss and Qwen, served through Groq, with Gemini as a fallback), a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool server, SQLite storage, and a local semantic search index over the NASA PDFs (MiniLM embeddings).
  • Infrastructure: a Debian VPS with nginx and Let’s Encrypt; every push to main deploys itself within about a minute and rolls back automatically if anything breaks.
  • Testing: GitHub Actions runs almost 400 tests on every change, plus headless browser checks on desktop and phone layouts.
  • Hardware: our own laptops and one small server.

What makes it creative

We didn’t stop at a simulator, and we didn’t stop at a database: we put them on the same screen. The gap map turns 24 scattered NASA studies into one picture you can understand in a few seconds, and it makes the missing tests visible instead of hiding them. Running a real CFD fire model on a phone, with no install, was a challenge we set ourselves. And the SI doesn’t only answer: it points at the page, changes the scenario and cites the exact NASA document.

What we considered

  • Honesty: Black Fox is a screening tool. It doesn’t replace NASA-STD-6001 testing, and the site says so. Gaps in the data are shown, never hidden, and the SI has to cite a source for every claim.
  • Gravity: NASA has almost no partial-gravity fire data, so we state where results come from microgravity or Earth gravity instead of guessing.
  • Accessibility: it works on weak phones, it’s in English and Hungarian, and there’s a beginner quick-start for people new to the topic.
  • Trust and cost: open models mean no lock-in, the whole system can run on a customer’s own servers, and it costs us about $130 a year to run.
  • Audience: aerospace engineers, researchers, professors and students: anyone deciding what to read, test or build next.
